an1.198:1.1: Cūḷapanthaka was slow of understanding, rejected even by his brother Mahāpanthaka, but then, supported by the Buddha, he achieved mastery ([thag10.4]()). He was praised at [ud5.10](), and gave effective instruction to the nuns at [pli-tv-bu-vb-pc22:1.1]().
an1.199:1.1: “Evolution of heart” (_cetovivaṭṭa_) and “evolution of perception” (_saññāvivaṭṭa_) are obscure terms. Perhaps “evolution of heart” refers to Cūḷapanthaka’s remarkable transformation. The late canonical Paṭisambhidamagga, on the other hand, explains “evolution of heart” as wisdom regarding manifoldness, perhaps in reference to Cūḷapanthaka’s creating a thousand mind-made bodies, and  “evolution of perception” as wisdom regarding “rushing upon” (_adhipatattā_), perhaps in reference to Mahāpanthaka’s headlong rush to awakening ([ps1.0:44.1]()).
an1.200:1.1: His verses are at [thag8.3](), where he tells of undertaking the resolve to not sit down until awakened.
an1.201:1.1: It seems Subhūti’s support of his fellow monk Saddha ([an11.14]()) was why he was foremost in non-strife ([mn139:14.3]()); he was additionally praised as worthy of donations. Subhūti’s meditation is praised at [ud6.7](), and his verse opens the Theragāthā at [thag1.1]().
an1.203:1.1: His verses are at [thag14.1](), with another isolated one at [thag1.42]().
an1.204:1.1: Praised at [ud5.7](), his verse at [thag1.3](), his doubts regarding points of Vinaya resolved by the Buddha at [pli-tv-kd6:16.1.1]().
an1.205:1.1: According to his verses ([thag13.1]()), he was former footman to the king of Aṅga. Raised in luxury, his overexertion in meditation was addressed with the famous simile of the harp ([pli-tv-kd5](), [an6.55]()). | His second name is quite uncertain. The commentary says it is a clan name, proposing the spelling _koṭivessa_, the most powerful of the merchants. The Sanskrit spelling is _koṭīviṃśa_, said to be an epithet due to receiving a gift of “twenty ounces” of gold. Neither of these seem particularly persuasive.
an1.206:1.1: Given the going forth by Mahākaccāna, he undertook the arduous journey from Avanti to visit the Buddha, where he recited the Chapter of the Eights ([ud5.6](), [pli-tv-kd5:13.9.5]()). His verses are at [thag5.11](). There is no evidence that his pointy ears indicate an elven ancestry.
an1.207:1.1: His verse is at [thag1.60](). No story to explain this epithet is found in the early texts, but he is much revered in Theravada.
an1.208:1.1: This quality is referenced at [snp5.19:16.1](), and his verses are at [thag5.8](). But he is best known for his extreme devotion to the Buddha while terminally ill ([sn22.87]()).
